turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hello Doctor. Thank you for fitting me in. It’s... well, it’s a little hard to explain exactly where to start, but I just feel like I’m always, always up and moving. I mean, I’m 70 years old, I haven't worked in years, so you'd think I’d be relaxing and enjoying my time, wouldn't you? 

But even on a completely quiet day when I have absolutely nowhere to be, I just can’t seem to settle down. I’ll start out with the best of intentions, sitting at the kitchen table to look over the garden club list—because I’m helping organize the spring luncheon this year and we have so many new members to keep track of—but then before I’ve even gotten halfway down the page, I’m up and digging through my knitting bag. I’m trying to finish this lovely yellow cardigan for my grandniece, you see. But then I don't even finish a single row of the pattern before I’m suddenly up again, pulling out all my travel papers and itineraries for a little trip I’m supposed to be taking next month. 

I’m just bouncing from the garden club list to my knitting bag to the travel papers, just pacing around the house, and before I know it the whole afternoon is gone and I haven't really finished any one thing. It's just... it's exhausting, honestly, always being in motion like this when I really just want to sit and enjoy a quiet morning.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain focus on tasks like reading a list or knitting, constantly switching activities without finishing any of them.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient reports feeling unable to settle down and describes herself as 'just pacing around the house,' indicating physical restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S013: The patient expresses frustration that she cannot simply sit and enjoy a quiet morning or engage peacefully in her leisure activities.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly states she is 'always, always up and moving' and describes the exhaustion of 'always being in motion.'

turns.doctor_question: Has this feeling of being constantly on the go and jumping between tasks been a lifelong pattern for you, or is it a more recent change?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, goodness... no, no, it’s certainly not a recent change. Not at all. It’s funny you ask that, because I was actually just thinking about this the other day when I was looking through some old keepsake boxes in the hall closet. I came across some of my old report cards from grade school—you know, the ones where the teachers would write those long, handwritten notes on the back in cursive? Well, my mother kept every single one of them, bless her heart. 

And looking at them, it just brought it all back. Even back then, way back in grade school, my teachers were telling my mother the exact same sorts of things. I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she actually pulled my mother aside after school one day and told her that I was a very bright girl, but just completely scattered. "Bright but scattered," that was the exact phrase she used. And it was true! Because I was always, always losing my papers. I’d shove my homework in my desk or my folder and it would just vanish into thin air, and I’d be in an absolute panic when it was time to turn it in. 

And the talking! I was always talking out of turn. If a thought popped into my head about the lesson, or even about something completely different like what we were having for lunch or a bird outside the window, I just had to say it right then and there. I couldn't seem to hold it in and raise my hand. And I was constantly wiggling in my seat. Just shifting around, swinging my legs, tapping my shoes on the floor... I could never seem to just sit still and get to the end of a worksheet. I’d be wiggling and looking around at what everyone else was doing long before I finished my work. 

My mother used to get so frustrated with me, constantly asking why I couldn't just sit quietly and focus like the other girls in my class. So, yes, this feeling has been with me my whole entire life, really. It’s just that now, at 70 years old, without a job to go to or children to chase after, you'd think I would have finally grown out of it and settled down, wouldn't you? But here I am, still wiggling and jumping around, just doing it in my own living room instead of Mrs. Gable's classroom.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient states she was always losing her papers and her homework would vanish into thin air.
